diagnostic.prompt: Which application_id values does this query return?
diagnostic.query:
SELECT application_id
FROM applications
WHERE member_id NOT IN (SELECT member_id FROM blocked_members)
ORDER BY application_id;
diagnostic.why: 101 is UNKNOWN because the list contains NULL; 102 is FALSE because it matches a value; 103 is UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only TRUE.

diagnostic.prompt: What is x in the following SELECT?
diagnostic.why: MAX without GROUP BY returns one row containing NULL for empty input.

diagnostic.prompt: What are the values of v in day_no ascending order?
diagnostic.query:
WITH t AS (SELECT 1 AS day_no, 10 AS amount UNION ALL SELECT 2, 20)
SELECT LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day_no) AS v FROM t ORDER BY day_no;
diagnostic.why: With ORDER BY, the default frame extends only through the current ordering key.

sections.title: WHERE subqueries
notes: WHERE keeps only rows whose condition evaluates to TRUE.
An empty scalar subquery evaluates to NULL. More than one row causes an error in MySQL.
IN is TRUE if any value matches. With no match and a NULL comparison, it is UNKNOWN.
ANY is TRUE if any comparison is TRUE and FALSE for empty input. ALL requires every comparison to be TRUE and is TRUE for empty input.
EXISTS checks whether any rows exist, regardless of their values.
Multi-column IN compares value combinations from the same row.
sections.pg: The basic patterns in this section also apply to PostgreSQL.

quizzes.prompt: What is x in the following SELECT?
quizzes.why: An empty scalar subquery evaluates to NULL.

quizzes.prompt: What is x in the following SELECT?
quizzes.why: ALL is TRUE when there are no values to compare. ANY would be FALSE.

quizzes.prompt: What is x in the following SELECT?
quizzes.query: SELECT 2 NOT IN (1, NULL) AS x;
quizzes.why: 2 = 1 is FALSE and 2 = NULL is UNKNOWN. The overall IN is UNKNOWN, and NOT leaves it UNKNOWN.

labs.prompt: Return all officers receiving the highest total pay. Exclude NULL pay. Order by officer_id ascending. Use a scalar subquery in WHERE.
labs.solution:
SELECT officer_id, total_pay
FROM payroll
WHERE total_pay = (SELECT MAX(total_pay) FROM payroll)
ORDER BY officer_id
labs.why: LIMIT 1 loses ties for the highest pay. MAX skips NULLs and returns NULL if every value is NULL. On large tables, inspect whether a total_pay index helps find the maximum and matching rows.
hint: There is one comparison value.
Compare each payment with the overall MAX in WHERE.

labs.prompt: Return offers in credit_offers whose amount is the maximum for their branch. Include ties and order by offer_id ascending. Use multi-column IN.
labs.solution:
SELECT offer_id, branch_id, amount
FROM credit_offers
WHERE (branch_id, amount) IN (
  SELECT branch_id, MAX(amount) FROM credit_offers GROUP BY branch_id
)
ORDER BY offer_id
labs.why: Separate IN checks for branch and amount can match another branch's maximum. All-NULL branches are excluded because comparison is UNKNOWN. Consider a (branch_id, amount) index.
hint: Preserve which branch owns each maximum.
Return branch_id and MAX(amount) together in the subquery.

labs.prompt: Classify the payment-account hierarchy: Root if no parent, Branch if it has a parent and children, otherwise Leaf. Order by node_id ascending. Use EXISTS.
labs.solution:
SELECT a.node_id, CASE
  WHEN a.parent_id IS NULL THEN 'Root'
  WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts b WHERE b.parent_id = a.node_id) THEN 'Branch'
  ELSE 'Leaf' END AS node_type
FROM accounts a
ORDER BY a.node_id
labs.why: Evaluate Root first so a childless root is not classified as Leaf. EXISTS preserves one row per account even with many children. Consider a parent_id index.
hint: Express classification precedence with CASE.
Check whether a row has the current node_id as its parent_id.
alternate: Rewrite using LEFT JOIN instead of EXISTS. Trade-off: with one million children, how do duplicate-removal and index-lookup costs change?

SELECT a.node_id, CASE WHEN a.parent_id IS NULL THEN 'Root' WHEN b.parent_id IS NOT NULL THEN 'Branch' ELSE 'Leaf' END AS node_type
FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT parent_id FROM accounts) b ON b.parent_id = a.node_id
ORDER BY a.node_id
EXISTS may stop at the first indexed match. DISTINCT and JOIN can process multiple parents together but may require scanning and deduplication.

sections.title: FROM / SELECT subqueries
notes: An inline view supplies a row set to the outer query through FROM.
An alias created inside can be referenced in the outer query block.
A scalar subquery in SELECT corresponds to one value per outer row.
COUNT returns 0 for empty input; SUM returns NULL.
ORDER BY inside an inline view alone does not guarantee final output order.
sections.pg: MySQL requires an alias for a derived table. PostgreSQL permits omission starting with version 16.

quizzes.prompt: Which statement runs in MySQL 8.0?
choices: SELECT * FROM (SELECT 1 AS n) AS d;
quizzes.why: A derived table in MySQL requires parentheses and an alias.

quizzes.prompt: What is x in the following SELECT?
quizzes.why: COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns one row containing 0 even for empty input.

quizzes.prompt: What is the result of this query in MySQL 8.0?
quizzes.query: SELECT (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 2) AS x;
quizzes.why: A scalar subquery in SELECT cannot return two rows.

labs.prompt: Find duplicate loan-underwriting job postings. Trim and lowercase addresses into address_key. Treat identical lender_id, role_id, and address_key combinations as the same posting. Exclude NULL or empty addresses and return combinations appearing at least twice. Order by lender_id, role_id, address_key ascending. Use an inline view.
labs.solution:
SELECT lender_id, role_id, address_key, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM (SELECT lender_id, role_id, LOWER(TRIM(address)) AS address_key FROM postings) p
WHERE address_key <> ''
GROUP BY lender_id, role_id, address_key
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY lender_id, role_id, address_key
labs.why: Grouping only by address merges different lenders and roles at the same address. If normalisation is expensive, store the normalised column and index it with lender_id.
hint: Separate normalisation and grouping.
Exclude empty strings before grouping.

labs.prompt: Calculate each representative's approved loan total and number of sales channels. Return only representatives with approved totals of at least 100 and at least two distinct channels. Do not count NULL channels. Order by rep_id ascending and use an inline view.
labs.solution:
SELECT rep_id, funded, channels
FROM (
  SELECT rep_id, SUM(amount) AS funded, COUNT(DISTINCT channel) AS channels
  FROM sales WHERE status = 'approved' GROUP BY rep_id
) s
WHERE funded >= 100 AND channels >= 2
ORDER BY rep_id
labs.why: COUNT(*) also counts repeated approvals from the same channel. Remove rejected loans before aggregation and compare plans using status and rep_id.
hint: Include only approved loans in the aggregation.
COUNT(DISTINCT channel) does not count NULL.

labs.prompt: Build a fraud-detection contest leaderboard. Sum each player's best score per challenge. Show 0 for players without submissions. Order by total_score descending, then player_id ascending. Use a scalar subquery in SELECT.
labs.solution:
SELECT p.player_id, COALESCE((
  SELECT SUM(b.best)
  FROM (SELECT player_id, challenge_id, MAX(score) AS best FROM attempts GROUP BY player_id, challenge_id) b
  WHERE b.player_id = p.player_id
), 0) AS total_score
FROM players p
ORDER BY total_score DESC, player_id
labs.why: Summing every submission double-counts challenges. Use COALESCE for an empty or all-NULL SUM. Consider an attempts index on (player_id, challenge_id, score).
hint: First reduce the aggregation to the highest score per challenge.
Convert SUM's NULL to 0, then specify tie ordering.
alternate: Rewrite using JOIN instead of a scalar subquery. Trade-off: which intermediate result can be reused as player counts grow?

SELECT p.player_id, COALESCE(SUM(b.best), 0) AS total_score
FROM players p
LEFT JOIN (SELECT player_id, challenge_id, MAX(score) AS best FROM attempts GROUP BY player_id, challenge_id) b ON b.player_id = p.player_id
GROUP BY p.player_id
ORDER BY total_score DESC, p.player_id
A JOIN can build challenge-level aggregates once and join them. Scalar queries may benefit from indexed lookups when retrieving only a few players. Compare actual plans.

sections.title: Subquery review
notes: Decide the aggregation unit and denominator first.
Explicitly alias outer columns in correlated subqueries.
Use NULLIF to define a ratio when its denominator is 0.
Distinguish exclusion of the current item from treatment of NULL ratings in peer averages.
Use the same rows with both x and y observed for correlation.
Normalise directions and remove duplicates before counting bidirectional relationships.
sections.pg: PostgreSQL supports CORR(y, x). In MySQL 8.0, Pearson correlation can be calculated from aggregates.

quizzes.prompt: What is ratio in the following SELECT?
quizzes.why: NULLIF(0, 0) returns NULL. Distinguish a ratio with no denominator from a ratio with a zero numerator.

quizzes.prompt: You predict a product's rating using peer ratings. What happens when unrated NULL values are passed directly to AVG?
choices: They are included in the denominator
They are excluded from both numerator and denominator
quizzes.why: AVG excludes NULLs. Replacing NULL with 0 changes the meaning of the average.

quizzes.prompt: Which rows should be used for the x and y aggregates in Pearson correlation?
choices: The same rows where both values are present
Rows with x and rows with y separately
All rows, always replacing missing values with 0
quizzes.why: Every aggregate must use the same complete pairs. Correlation is undefined if either variable has zero variance.

labs.prompt: Return every employee with the highest salary in their risk team. Exclude NULL salaries. Order by employee_id ascending. Use a correlated subquery.
labs.solution:
SELECT a.employee_id, a.team_id, a.salary
FROM staff a
WHERE a.salary = (SELECT MAX(b.salary) FROM staff b WHERE b.team_id = a.team_id)
ORDER BY a.employee_id
labs.why: Omitting the team condition finds the company-wide maximum. Preserve ties within teams. A (team_id, salary) index is a candidate.
hint: Pass the outer row's team to the inner aggregate.
Compare both team_id columns using explicit aliases.

labs.prompt: Calculate loan approval ratios for all registered branches. Include NULL-status applications in the denominator. Return NULL for branches without applications. Order by branch_id ascending.
labs.solution:
SELECT b.branch_id, a.approvals * 1.0 / NULLIF(a.total, 0) AS approval_rate
FROM branches b LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT branch_id, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'approved' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS approvals, COUNT(*) AS total
  FROM applications GROUP BY branch_id
) a ON a.branch_id = b.branch_id
ORDER BY b.branch_id
labs.why: COUNT(status) loses NULL-status applications from the denominator. INNER JOIN removes empty branches. Keep the result as a ratio and round only the final display when needed.
hint: Use the branch list as the base table.
Aggregate applications per branch first, then LEFT JOIN.

labs.prompt: Estimate ratings from the average of other products in the same product group. Exclude the current product and NULL ratings. Return NULL if no comparable rating exists. Order by product_id ascending.
labs.solution:
SELECT p.product_id, (
  SELECT AVG(q.rating) FROM products q WHERE q.segment_id = p.segment_id AND q.product_id <> p.product_id
) AS predicted
FROM products p
ORDER BY p.product_id
labs.why: AVG(DISTINCT rating) incorrectly removes different products sharing a rating. Precomputing group SUM and COUNT can reduce repeated lookups compared with per-product comparisons.
hint: Require both matching product group and different product ID.
AVG excludes NULLs and returns NULL for empty input.
alternate: Rewrite using a window instead of a correlated subquery. Trade-off: how does retrieving a few products differ from processing all products?

SELECT product_id, (SUM(rating) OVER w - COALESCE(rating, 0)) * 1.0 / NULLIF(COUNT(rating) OVER w - CASE WHEN rating IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END, 0) AS predicted
FROM products
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY segment_id)
ORDER BY product_id
A window reuses group sums and counts. For a few products, an indexed correlated lookup may do less work than processing the full window.

sections.title: Window aggregate functions
notes: Windows preserve input rows.
Without PARTITION BY, all rows form one partition.
Window input consists of rows after WHERE and GROUP BY.
ORDER BY inside OVER defines calculation order. Final output requires a separate ORDER BY.
SUM, AVG, and COUNT(column) ignore NULLs. COUNT(*) counts rows.
For row-by-row running values, use a unique ordering key and an explicit ROWS frame.
sections.pg: The basic patterns in this section also apply to PostgreSQL.

quizzes.prompt: What is n on each row of the following SELECT?
quizzes.query: WITH t AS (SELECT 1 AS x UNION ALL SELECT NULL) SELECT COUNT(x) OVER () AS n FROM t;
quizzes.why: OVER () treats both rows as one partition. COUNT(x) does not count NULL.

quizzes.prompt: If WHERE keeps only approved transactions before a window calculation, what happens to rejected transactions?
choices: They are included in the window
They are excluded from the window input
They are included only in the window ordering
quizzes.why: WHERE is evaluated before the window calculation.

quizzes.prompt: How are window ORDER BY and final ORDER BY related?
choices: Window ORDER BY guarantees final order
The two ORDER BY clauses cannot be used together
Window ORDER BY defines calculation order; final order is specified separately
quizzes.why: Use ORDER BY in the outer SELECT to guarantee output order.

labs.prompt: For each payment, add its account's average transaction amount and count of transactions with recorded amounts. Retain NULL-amount rows and order by payment_id ascending.
labs.solution:
SELECT payment_id, AVG(amount) OVER w AS mean_amount, COUNT(amount) OVER w AS known_count
FROM payments
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY account_id)
ORDER BY payment_id
labs.why: COUNT(*) includes transactions with missing amounts. AVG(DISTINCT) loses separate payments with equal amounts. Use a named window to share the partition definition.
hint: Add aggregates to each row without collapsing transactions.
Apply the same PARTITION BY to both aggregates.

labs.prompt: Within each queue batch_id, pos is consecutive from 1. Swap ticket_id for adjacent positions (1 and 2, 3 and 4, etc.). Leave an unmatched final position unchanged. Order by batch_id, pos ascending. Use COUNT OVER for batch size.
labs.solution:
WITH sized AS (SELECT q.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY batch_id) AS n FROM queue q)
SELECT a.batch_id, a.pos, b.ticket_id
FROM sized a JOIN queue b ON b.batch_id = a.batch_id AND b.pos = CASE
  WHEN a.pos % 2 = 0 THEN a.pos - 1 WHEN a.pos < a.n THEN a.pos + 1 ELSE a.pos END
ORDER BY a.batch_id, a.pos
labs.why: Counting the whole table as one partition can seek a nonexistent partner at the end of an odd-sized batch. (batch_id, pos) must be unique; an index helps the JOIN.
hint: You need the final position in each batch.
Only an unmatched odd final row should use its own position as its partner.

labs.prompt: Process transfer requests within each batch in seq order. Amounts are positive and seq is unique within a batch. Return the last request with cumulative amount at most 100 and its cumulative amount. Exclude batches with no processable request. Order by batch_id ascending.
labs.solution:
WITH sums AS (
  SELECT batch_id, seq, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY batch_id ORDER BY seq ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total FROM transfers
)
SELECT s.batch_id, s.seq, s.running_total FROM sums s
WHERE s.running_total <= 100 AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM sums t WHERE t.batch_id = s.batch_id AND t.seq > s.seq AND t.running_total <= 100
)
ORDER BY s.batch_id
labs.why: Include exactly 100. Assuming consecutive seq values fails on gaps. Inspect access in (batch_id, seq) order.
hint: First add the cumulative amount within each batch.
Among rows within the limit, select the one with no later eligible row.
alternate: Calculate the running amount with a self JOIN instead of a window. Trade-off: how does the intermediate row count change for long batches?

WITH sums AS (SELECT a.batch_id, a.seq, SUM(b.amount) AS running_total
FROM transfers a JOIN transfers b ON b.batch_id = a.batch_id AND b.seq <= a.seq
GROUP BY a.batch_id, a.seq)
SELECT s.batch_id, s.seq, s.running_total FROM sums s
WHERE s.running_total <= 100 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sums t WHERE t.batch_id = s.batch_id AND t.seq > s.seq AND t.running_total <= 100)
ORDER BY s.batch_id
A self JOIN for a batch of n rows creates n(n+1)/2 pairs. A window can update cumulative state once per row after obtaining the input order.

sections.title: Window ranking functions
notes: ROW_NUMBER assigns a different number to every row, including ties.
RANK gives ties the same rank and leaves corresponding gaps afterwards.
DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank and continues without gaps.
If ROW_NUMBER's ordering is not unique, the order among tied rows is not guaranteed.
Apply rank filters in an outer query block after calculating the window.
sections.pg: MySQL places NULL first with ASC; PostgreSQL defaults to NULLS LAST with ASC. Use CASE or an IS NULL sort key for portable ordering.

quizzes.prompt: What does RANK return for scores 90,90,80 ordered descending?
quizzes.why: The first two rows rank first and the third ranks third.

quizzes.prompt: What r values does this query return?
quizzes.query:
WITH t AS (SELECT 9 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 8)
SELECT DISTINCT DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC) AS r FROM t ORDER BY r;
quizzes.why: DENSE_RANK assigns consecutive numbers to distinct ordering keys.

quizzes.prompt: Which function selects exactly two rows, choosing smaller agent_id first for ties?
choices: ROW_NUMBER ORDER BY score DESC, agent_id
quizzes.why: Give ROW_NUMBER a unique ordering to control both row count and tie order.

labs.prompt: Return the first login for each account. Choose the smallest day_no, breaking same-day ties with the smallest event_id. Order by account_id ascending. Use ROW_NUMBER.
labs.solution:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT l.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY day_no, event_id) AS rn FROM logins l)
SELECT account_id, day_no, event_id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY account_id
labs.why: Joining only on MIN(day_no) duplicates accounts with multiple first-day logins. Keep event_id as a tie-breaker and consider an (account_id, day_no, event_id) index.
hint: Find the first row within each account.
Include both date and event ID in the window order.

labs.prompt: Return employees in the top two distinct score bands per team. Include all ties and exclude NULL scores. Order by team_id, band, agent_id ascending. Use DENSE_RANK.
labs.solution:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT s.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY team_id ORDER BY score DESC) AS band FROM scores s WHERE score IS NOT NULL)
SELECT team_id, agent_id, score, band FROM ranked WHERE band <= 2 ORDER BY team_id, band, agent_id
labs.why: Adding agent_id to window ORDER BY splits ties. Use it only for final output order. Filter NULL scores before ranking.
hint: Select two score bands, not two employees.
Separate display order from ranking criteria.

labs.prompt: For each card, sum all rows in its first recorded sales month as first_amount. month_no increases continuously across years. Exclude NULL amounts when identifying launch. Order by card_id ascending and use RANK.
labs.solution:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT s.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY card_id ORDER BY month_no) AS r FROM card_sales s WHERE amount IS NOT NULL)
SELECT card_id, month_no AS first_month, SUM(amount) AS first_amount
FROM ranked WHERE r = 1 GROUP BY card_id, month_no ORDER BY card_id
labs.why: ROW_NUMBER keeps only one sale from the first month. Exclude NULLs before ranking; 0 is a recorded sale. Consider a (card_id, month_no) index.
hint: Give every row in the first month the same rank.
Separate NULL filtering, ranking, and first-month aggregation.
alternate: Rewrite using a correlated subquery instead of a window. Trade-off: how does a (card_id, month_no) index help each approach?

SELECT s.card_id, s.month_no AS first_month, SUM(s.amount) AS first_amount
FROM card_sales s WHERE s.amount IS NOT NULL AND s.month_no = (SELECT MIN(t.month_no) FROM card_sales t WHERE t.card_id = s.card_id AND t.amount IS NOT NULL)
GROUP BY s.card_id, s.month_no ORDER BY s.card_id
The window may reduce sorting cost using card-month order. A correlated query can seek each card's earliest month, but check repeated lookups and the cost of skipping NULL amounts.

sections.title: Window positional functions
notes: LAG and LEAD reference neighbouring rows within an ordered partition.
The previous observed date is not necessarily yesterday. Check the date difference too.
LAG's default applies only when the referenced row does not exist. An existing row with a NULL value still returns NULL.
FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE read the first and last values of the current frame within the partition.
For duplicate timestamps, first aggregate to the desired unit or specify a tie-breaker.
sections.pg: The basic patterns in this section also apply to PostgreSQL.

quizzes.prompt: What does LAG(x, 1, 0) return on the first row and on a row whose predecessor's x is NULL, respectively?
quizzes.why: The default applies only when the reference position is out of bounds.

quizzes.prompt: What are the next_x values in x ascending order for the following SELECT?
quizzes.query: WITH t AS (SELECT 4 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 9) SELECT LEAD(x) OVER (ORDER BY x) AS next_x FROM t ORDER BY x;
quizzes.why: LEAD reads the next row, so the final row returns NULL.

quizzes.prompt: What does the presence of LAG(day_no) alone tell you?
choices: There is a previous observed row
There was definitely a transaction yesterday
quizzes.why: It only indicates a preceding row in the sort order. Check the date difference to establish whether it was yesterday.

labs.prompt: Return account dates whose balance increased from the previous calendar day. day_no is a consecutive integer date, with at most one row per account per day. Compare only when yesterday's observation exists. Order by account_id, day_no ascending.
labs.solution:
WITH prev AS (SELECT b.*, LAG(day_no) OVER w AS prev_day, LAG(amount) OVER w AS prev_amount FROM balances b WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY day_no))
SELECT account_id, day_no, amount FROM prev
WHERE day_no = prev_day + 1 AND amount > prev_amount ORDER BY account_id, day_no
labs.why: Exclude increases when the previous observation was two days earlier. Replacing NULL with 0 may invent an increase. Inspect sorting costs by account and date.
hint: Retrieve both date and amount from the previous row.
Check both a date difference of 1 and an increase in amount.

labs.prompt: For each gateway, return the middle event_id when three consecutive events share a code. event_id is unique within gateway_id; ignore numeric gaps. NULL codes do not match. Order by gateway_id, event_id ascending and use LAG and LEAD.
labs.solution:
WITH neighbors AS (SELECT e.*, LAG(code) OVER w AS before_code, LEAD(code) OVER w AS after_code FROM events e WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY gateway_id ORDER BY event_id))
SELECT gateway_id, event_id, code FROM neighbors WHERE code = before_code AND code = after_code ORDER BY gateway_id, event_id
labs.why: Consecutive means adjacent in sorted order. Joining on event_id + 1 fails with gaps. NULL code comparisons evaluate to UNKNOWN.
hint: Look in both directions from the middle row.
Share one partition definition between LAG and LEAD.

labs.prompt: Add the application's first and final status to every review event. event_id is a unique chronological key. Preserve NULL if the final status is NULL. Order by application_id, event_id ascending.
labs.solution:
SELECT application_id, event_id, FIRST_VALUE(status) OVER w AS first_status, LAST_VALUE(status) OVER w AS last_status
FROM reviews WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY event_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)
ORDER BY application_id, event_id
labs.why: With the default frame, LAST_VALUE usually returns the current row's status. UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING reaches the partition end. Order by event_id, not status.
hint: Find the first and last events across the entire partition.
Check the endpoint of the frame visible to LAST_VALUE.
alternate: Replace FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE with scalar subqueries. Trade-off: how does the cost differ for one application versus all events?

SELECT a.application_id, a.event_id, (SELECT b.status FROM reviews b WHERE b.application_id = a.application_id ORDER BY b.event_id LIMIT 1) AS first_status, (SELECT b.status FROM reviews b WHERE b.application_id = a.application_id ORDER BY b.event_id DESC LIMIT 1) AS last_status
FROM reviews a ORDER BY a.application_id, a.event_id
With an index, endpoints for a few applications can be found quickly. For all events, consider reusing a window or per-application aggregate instead of repeatedly retrieving the same two statuses.

sections.title: Window frame
notes: ROWS defines boundaries by positions in the ordered rows.
RANGE defines boundaries by ordering-key values and peers.
With ORDER BY, the default frame is RANGE from UNBOUNDED PRECEDING through CURRENT ROW.
Without ORDER BY, the default frame is the entire partition.
LAST_VALUE's default frame excludes rows with later ordering keys.
A seven-day range contains today and the preceding six days. With missing dates, seven rows differ from seven days.
sections.pg: For DATE keys, MySQL uses INTERVAL 6 DAY and PostgreSQL uses INTERVAL '6 days'. For the integer day_no here, use RANGE 6 PRECEDING.

quizzes.prompt: Two rows share day_no with amounts 4 and 6, and no earlier rows exist. What does SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day_no) return?
quizzes.why: In the default RANGE frame, CURRENT ROW includes all peers with the same day_no.

quizzes.prompt: What is v for the row where x = 10 in the following SELECT?
quizzes.query: WITH t AS (SELECT 10 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 20) SELECT x, LAST_VALUE(x) OVER (ORDER BY x) AS v FROM t;
quizzes.why: The default frame ends at the current ordering key, so 20 is outside it.

quizzes.prompt: Which frame suits a calendar-based seven-day aggregate over payment logs with missing dates?
quizzes.why: If 6 PRECEDING counts rows, missing dates can make the frame extend further into the past.

labs.prompt: Deposits on the same date share a cumulative total including every deposit that day. Return each payment_id and that total in payment_id ascending order. Use RANGE.
labs.solution: SELECT payment_id, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day_no RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS cumulative FROM deposits ORDER BY payment_id
labs.why: ROWS may give same-day rows different totals. Adding payment_id to window ORDER BY splits peers. Consider a date index.
hint: Keep rows sharing a date in one peer group.
Use payment_id only for final output ordering.

labs.prompt: Calculate each account's seven-day moving sum on each observed date. day_no is an integer date with at most one row per account per day. Do not add rows for missing dates. Order by account_id, day_no ascending and use RANGE.
labs.solution: SELECT account_id, day_no, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY day_no RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_sum FROM daily ORDER BY account_id, day_no
labs.why: A seven-row window skips missing dates and can include transactions older than seven days. With one row per day, an (account_id, day_no) index is suitable.
hint: Determine how far the frame starts before the current day_no.
Specify both the account partition and RANGE boundaries.

labs.prompt: For each merchant's observed dates, return the seven-day moving sum and average over observed daily totals. Aggregate same-day payments first. An all-NULL day has a NULL daily total and is excluded from the average denominator. Order by merchant_id, day_no ascending. Use RANGE.
labs.solution:
WITH daily AS (SELECT merchant_id, day_no, SUM(amount) AS amount FROM captures GROUP BY merchant_id, day_no)
SELECT merchant_id, day_no, SUM(amount) OVER w AS rolling_sum, AVG(amount) OVER w AS rolling_avg
FROM daily WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY day_no RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY merchant_id, day_no
labs.why: Averaging transaction rows directly weights days with more transactions more heavily. Filling missing or all-NULL days with 0 changes the denominator. Consider daily pre-aggregation for large datasets.
hint: First reduce the data to one row per merchant per day.
Share the seven-day frame between SUM and AVG.
alternate: Use a self JOIN on daily aggregates instead of RANGE. Trade-off: how do costs change when extending the period from 7 to 90 days?

WITH daily AS (SELECT merchant_id, day_no, SUM(amount) AS amount FROM captures GROUP BY merchant_id, day_no)
SELECT a.merchant_id, a.day_no, SUM(b.amount) AS rolling_sum, AVG(b.amount) AS rolling_avg
FROM daily a JOIN daily b ON a.merchant_id = b.merchant_id AND b.day_no BETWEEN a.day_no - 6 AND a.day_no
GROUP BY a.merchant_id, a.day_no ORDER BY a.merchant_id, a.day_no
Longer periods increase matching pairs in the self JOIN. A RANGE window can maintain its interval within an ordered partition.

quizzes.prompt: You found each card product's first sales year and must retain every row in that year. What is n in the following result?
quizzes.query:
WITH sales AS (SELECT 2024 AS yr UNION ALL SELECT 2024 UNION ALL SELECT 2025), ranked AS (SELECT RANK() OVER (ORDER BY yr) AS r FROM sales)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM ranked WHERE r = 1;
quizzes.why: The two first-year rows share an ordering key, so both rank first.

quizzes.prompt: What is the maximum number of contributing rows in ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW?
quizzes.why: The previous six rows plus the current row. There are fewer near the start of a partition.

labs.prompt: Find settlement counterparties. Exclude accounts with the same (provider_id, account_ref) in the payout restriction list. NULL in the list matches no account. Order by account_id ascending.
labs.solution: SELECT a.account_id FROM beneficiaries a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM restrictions r WHERE r.provider_id = a.provider_id AND r.account_ref = a.account_ref) ORDER BY a.account_id
labs.why: NOT IN can become UNKNOWN when the list contains NULL. Check provider and reference together. Consider a composite index.
hint: Find accounts with no restricted row sharing both keys.
Consider NOT EXISTS comparing both keys together.

labs.prompt: Return each customer's number of distinct referral friends. Relationships are bidirectional; exclude reverse duplicates and self-links. Return 0 for customers without relationships. Order by customer_id ascending.
labs.solution:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(r.friend_id) AS friend_count
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT src AS customer_id, dst AS friend_id FROM referrals WHERE src <> dst UNION SELECT dst, src FROM referrals WHERE src <> dst) r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id
labs.why: UNION ALL recounts reverse duplicates. COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN gives isolated customers a count of 1. Consider a normalised unique key when storing relationships.
hint: Create both customer-to-friend directions.
Expand directions, deduplicate, then LEFT JOIN to the customer list.

labs.prompt: Return Pearson correlation between loan amount x and loss y as corr. Use only complete pairs. Return NULL when either variance is 0 or no comparable pairs exist.
labs.solution:
SELECT (n * sxy - sx * sy) * 1.0 / NULLIF(SQRT((n * sxx - sx * sx) * (n * syy - sy * sy)), 0) AS corr
FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(x) AS sx, SUM(y) AS sy, SUM(x * y) AS sxy, SUM(x * x) AS sxx, SUM(y * y) AS syy FROM observations WHERE x IS NOT NULL AND y IS NOT NULL) s
labs.why: Use the same pairs in every statistic. For large values, consider sum-of-squares overflow and cancellation error. Compare a mean-centred calculation too.
hint: Filter to complete pairs once.
The Pearson numerator is nΣxy − ΣxΣy. The denominator is the square root of the product of the two variance terms.

labs.prompt: Return the starting month of each period in which an analyst published payment-security reports for three consecutive months. Multiple reports in one month count once. Four consecutive months yield two start months. Order by analyst_id, start_month ascending.
labs.solution:
WITH months AS (SELECT DISTINCT analyst_id, month_no FROM reports), next_months AS (SELECT analyst_id, month_no, LEAD(month_no, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY analyst_id ORDER BY month_no) AS second_next FROM months)
SELECT analyst_id, month_no AS start_month FROM next_months WHERE second_next = month_no + 2 ORDER BY analyst_id, start_month
labs.why: Without deduplication, the row two positions ahead cannot establish three consecutive months. Consider an (analyst_id, month_no) index.
hint: Deduplicate at the month level.
Check whether the observation two rows ahead is exactly two months later.

labs.prompt: Chargebacks are recorded by merchant. Add the count of chargebacks with non-NULL amounts within the seven-day date range to every row. Same-day rows receive the same count. Order by merchant_id, case_id ascending.
labs.solution: SELECT merchant_id, case_id, COUNT(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY merchant_id ORDER BY day_no RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS known_count FROM chargebacks ORDER BY merchant_id, case_id
labs.why: COUNT(*) includes NULL amounts. Keep same-date peers together so their seven-day ranges agree. Consider merchant-level ordering and the proportion of missing amounts.
hint: Define frame boundaries by date.
Pass the amount column to COUNT.
